paragraphs.text: Mi Lan Xiang is one of the traditional [ten aroma types](dancong:aromas) by which [Phoenix Dancong](dancong:definition) is sorted and sold, and [one of the most widely made](dancong:mi-lan-xiang). The name comes from the bush and the making, not from anything added, and it covers a range of teas rather than one. [Dancong](dancong:name) means single bush. Today a named line is mostly grown from cuttings or grafts of a chosen bush, so one name no longer means one tree.

The leaf comes from [Phoenix Mountain](phoenix-mountain:where-it-is), Fenghuang Shan, a range in Chao'an, Chaozhou, in eastern Guangdong. There tea grows from the low foothills up to roughly 1,100 metres. Cloud and mist sit on the upper slopes for much of the year and the nights are cool, so [the bushes grow slowly](phoenix-mountain:mist-and-climate), which the trade links to the character of the leaf. The leaf is withered in the sun, then [shaken and rested in rounds](dancong:making) to bruise its edges, the step that gives each type its character. It is then fixed at high heat, rolled into long dark strips, dried, and roasted as it is refined.

brewing.text: Brew it gongfu style in a small gaiwan or clay pot, with about 3 to 8 grams for 100 to 120 ml and hot water, about 88 to 100°C; Chinese accounts mostly say 95 to 100°C. A quick rinse is common. Steeps start at a few seconds and grow a few seconds each round, and a good Dancong gives about eight to fifteen. Too long, too hot or too much leaf and it turns bitter and astringent.

notice.text: Flowers above all, a sweetness that comes back after swallowing, a high scent that lasts, honey, often ripe fruit such as peach, and what the trade calls mountain rhyme, shan yun; a liquor from golden to orange-red or amber.

unsupported.sentence: The name comes from the bush and the making, not from anything added, and it covers a range of teas rather than one.

unsupported.why: The claims say the scent comes from the bush and the making, and that the aroma type is named for the flower, fruit or spice the scent recalls. They never say the name comes from the bush and the making.

unsupported.sentence: The leaf is withered in the sun, then shaken and rested in rounds to bruise its edges, the step that gives each type its character.
unsupported.words: the step that gives each type its character
unsupported.why: The making claim says only that shaking and resting bruises the leaf edge and builds the scent. The claims credit the bush and the roast as main differences between teas, and no claim says this step gives each aroma type its character.
